Deadline 11 days away, sales brochure only just received – insufficient time to consider

Ms. Au, owner of Wang Tai Court, lives with her husband, three sons and a domestic helper. Her family is among the few who have decided not to return the acquisition proposal letter before 31 August. Ms. Au said she understands and knows they will inevitably have to sell their property in the future, but believes that before 31 August, both physically and mentally, she is not ready to make this decision.

As a mother of three, her family is her top priority — all three sons study in Tai Po, and she hopes as much as possible not to disrupt their lives, wanting to find a home similar to Wang Fuk Court in the same district and rebuild a stable home. However, she has yet to find an option that suits her family's needs — the sales brochure and detailed price list for the "Special Sales Scheme" were only released on 20 August, making it difficult for her to digest and consider the vast amount of information in a short time. Meanwhile, the western estate on Chung Nga Road has poor transport connections and will not be ready for occupation until 2030; buying a second-hand Home Ownership Scheme flat in Tai Po means she and her sons may not be able to bear the shadow of another major maintenance; as for taking the money to the private market, she still carries an existing mortgage that cannot be transferred, making it unaffordable and difficult to find a home suitable for a family of six.

Each of the three options has its limitations. Ms. Au said helplessly, "They gave me all the options so late — I simply don't have enough time to consider this. I don't have the confidence to choose a suitable plan for my family, and I'm not mentally ready to sign this letter of intent." "It's not whether I want to or whether I would consider it — it's that I simply cannot decide⋯ I cannot rashly make such a major decision for my family."

Facing risk: worry and disappointment

In recent days, various parties have been reminding owners about the 31 August deadline — the Wang Fuk Court Acquisition Company Limited sent a letter earlier stating that failing to return the letter of intent before the deadline would be regarded as forfeiting participation in the long-term housing arrangement scheme; Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun also spoke up, saying the deadline is a "serious timeline" and will not be extended, and that legislation to resume ownership would be considered, with compensation expected to be "significantly less" than the government's acquisition price.

Afraid of collapsing under the mental pressure

Ms. Au understands the government needs to set a deadline to act, but as a disaster victim, she finds it painful and disappointing that the government often speaks of "putting people's feelings first" while also stating that "once any decision is made, there's no going back." She does not shy away from admitting she worries about the risks she will have to bear and indeed feels tremendous pressure, but at this stage, "I really cannot force myself to make this decision," "I am very afraid of making the wrong decision, and also very afraid that I will not be able to bear the mental pressure and collapse."

Ms. Au had also considered returning the letter of intent first, but she said that after the 30 June deadline, some residents reported that they only learned upon signing that the terms included giving up items inside the flat and not being allowed to photocopy the sale and purchase agreement, which made her worry about facing unacceptable terms.

Ms. Au reiterated that since the government announced the acquisition, she and her husband had been monitoring the prices of Tai Po estates and had asked the explanation team about estate insurance and maintenance information, but never received a reply. With the government drip-feeding different pieces of information through meetings, the deadline is now imminent — "As an owner, both physically and mentally, I am not ready to make such a major decision in such a short time."

Hoping for extension, waiting for investigation report before selling the flat

Although the government has stated it will not extend the deadline, Ms. Au still hopes the government can stand in the disaster victims' shoes and understand that this is "a lifelong shadow," truly putting "people's feelings first," and grant flexibility and room according to different residents' needs by extending the deadline, giving them enough time to carefully consider and make important, long-term decisions for their families that they will not regret.

She has also always believed that, in principle, the sale of the property should wait until the investigation report is released, to clarify the cause and responsibility of the fire. She also finds it difficult to accept using donated funds to acquire the property. However, the independent committee has already been granted an extension and is expected to complete its report only at the end of October.

"As a resident, what I find very hard to let go of is that I want there to be a proper sequence — let me understand why this happened at Wang Fuk, why we had to suffer this misfortune, and then tell me what choices I have, that I need to take a step forward, that I cannot return to Wang Fuk. I feel that with this sequence, as a resident, I would feel more at ease, more able to accept selling a place I love so much."

"Not being able to wait until the independent investigation report is released before selling the flat is, for me, a regret."

Even if reluctant, must build a new home

The government recently announced that 94.7% of owners have returned their letters, with only about a hundred households outstanding. Ms. Au said the numbers are meaningless to her, as whether to sell the property is decided by each family's needs — "it's not a game of minority服从多數." She also frankly said it is difficult to predict what will happen after 31 August: "If they really insist on acting according to the law first rather than what they call putting feelings first, there's nothing I can do. I'm forced to just accept it and see how things develop."

Regarding Wong Wai-lun's remark that some owners have not returned their letters because they are dissatisfied with the acquisition price, Ms. Au said this is not her thinking, and she stressed she is not trying to go against the government. She has always believed that the most responsible decision for her family is to see the road ahead clearly before deciding. If she can find a suitable plan, "I am actually quite willing to sign this letter of intent."

Having frequently mentioned in past interviews how much she loves Wang Fuk Court and the bonds with fellow residents, Ms. Au frankly said she understands deeply that things cannot be reversed, and selling the property is the only option — "whether I am willing or not, it is my only option." Letting go of Wang Fuk and moving away is an inevitable fact and a decision made out of helplessness: "Even if I can't bear to leave, I have to take a step forward for myself and rebuild a new home⋯ Some things really require moving forward, some things require acceptance."

"As long as the people are home, the home is there" — this is what she has often told her three sons since the disaster. "I hope that even if the residents can't bear to leave Wang Fuk, they will let it go and move forward to start a new life."
